How measured risk becomes money

How measuring a payments bank’s risks changes what $10.0m can achieve

How to read this case

Start with the Before page to see the bank’s risk register, matrix and loss records as reconstructed for this case. Method explains the measurement of the same 100 risks, and After shows how the estimates and rankings change. Budget compares what $10.0m buys under each ranking, including checks against the underlying model values. Controls and Steps explain the decisions, and Money follows the selected plan into the accounts. Governance describes responsibility for those decisions. Your version sets out a twelve-week pilot on one of your own registers.

Terms used in this case

Operational risk
The risk of losing money when a process, a system, a person or an outside event fails. A payment sent to the wrong account is one example, and a platform outage is another.
RCSA
RCSA stands for risk and control self-assessment. Risk owners meet every quarter, rate each risk on a matrix and record how well its controls work.
Workshop
The quarterly RCSA meeting where the risk owners rate each risk on the matrix.
Risk matrix
A grid that rates each risk by how likely it is and how much damage it would do. Every cell has a colour, and the colour decides how much attention the risk gets.
Control
A check or process that makes a loss less likely or smaller, such as a second person approving a large payment. A key control is one the bank relies on for its financial reporting or a regulatory obligation.
Expected loss
The average yearly loss from a risk, with frequent small losses and rare large ones counted together.
Typical loss
The median loss per event: half of events cost less and half cost more. Expected loss uses the average, which includes the contribution of rare, large events.
Bad-year loss
The total yearly loss that the bank should expect to exceed about once every twenty years.
Band
One of the four ranges the matrix offers for likelihood or for impact, such as a loss of $1.0m to $10.0m.
Book of work
The projects the bank could fund this year. The reconstructed register contains 100 proposals, one for each risk. One is an already approved programme, leaving 99 projects to compete for the remediation budget.
Measured return
The measured loss a project removes in a year for each dollar it costs in a year. A return of $6.12 means the project removes $6.12 of expected loss for each dollar.
Colour plan
The 16 projects the bank funded before the measurement, chosen by matrix colour. The Steps and Money pages call it the original plan.
Chosen plan
The 24 projects the committee funded in order of measured return, with one recorded exception.
Range
An uncertainty interval with a target coverage of four in five. Checks within the case model show how often it contains the underlying model value.
Risk appetite
The level of loss the board has agreed to carry.
Net value
What a plan or a step takes off the yearly cost of operational risk, compared with the original plan.
Remediation budget
The money the bank spends each year on the projects in its book of work. Cardinal’s research calls it the mitigation budget. Across the research simulations, ranking projects by measured size reduces the budget needed for the same protection by an average of 60%. That saving applies to this budget alone.
Budget-equivalent saving
The share of the remediation budget the bank could hand back and still get the same protection, once it ranks its projects better. It is the headline measure in Cardinal's research, where it averages 60%.
Model value
The loss value assigned to a risk in the numerical reconstruction. It lets us check the rankings and uncertainty intervals against a known value within the model. The source bank’s actual risk remains uncertain.
Rerun
One of 600 model runs using different random draws for workshop ratings, comparisons and ranking ties. The runs show how much the calculated result varies.
Key risk indicator
A number the bank watches to spot a risk as it grows, such as a count of failed reconciliations. Banks usually shorten it to KRI.
Total cost of operational risk
What the bank spends on its controls and projects in a year plus the losses it expects in that year.

The bank’s register in the reconstructed case

The bank's risk matrix

Each dot represents a risk, and the corner number counts the risks in that box. Rows show likelihood and columns show the cost of one event, after controls. Scores run from one for Rare likelihood or Low impact to four for High likelihood or Critical impact. The sum sets the colour: four or less is green, five is amber, and six or more is red.

How a risk gets its place on the matrix and its dollar figure

How the bank turned ratings into dollars

LikelihoodWhat the rating meansFrequency used
ImpactLoss per eventLoss used
The matrix uses the rating after controls, usually called the residual rating. When a risk has a regulatory impact, the workshop takes the higher of its financial and regulatory impact bands. The calculation then converts that band to dollars using the table above. Risk colour also sets the testing cycle: quarterly for red, twice a year for amber and annually for green. Project priorities follow the scores behind the colours, so the Budget page’s comparison of $47.3m with $24.1m is independent of this dollar conversion. Recalibrating a band changes its representative value while giving every risk in that band the same value; the High impact band spans $1.0m to $10.0m. The source case also includes scenario analysis for a small number of large risks in the capital model. Those scenarios sit outside this register analysis.

The bank's own figures for one year

The case reflects a gap the bank had identified between its matrix figures and loss records, alongside concern about AI-enabled fraud with little loss history. The Method page explains the comparison of the same 100 risks in dollars.

Each risk is compared with 14 others

The method asks judges which of two risks is more likely and which would cost more. In the reconstructed case, each risk meets 14 others on each question, giving 1,400 comparisons in total. Seven reference risks with known frequency or cost set the measurement scales. The case model simulates these comparisons and their uncertainty. In use, the bank checks the resulting estimates against its losses and repeats the measurement each quarter. The seven tabs explain the stages.

Five years of loss records provide a limited sample. New risks may have no recorded events, and a risk that occurs once in thirty years often leaves no event in that period. The measurement estimates losses for these risks as well.

Three options for the committee

The case combines a revised project ranking with evidence about control costs and effects. It gives the Business Control Committee three options, from taking the savings in cash to reinvesting them, and uses the middle option for the main comparison. The Business Control Officer, or BCO, is responsible for the controls and approves smaller changes. Select an option to load its steps, or switch individual steps on and off to explore a different plan.

    Responsibility for the decisions

    The case follows the bank’s existing decision structure. Cardinal supplies measurements for the business owners and committees to consider. The register, risk categories and RCSA calendar remain in place. Responsibilities follow the three lines of defence across the business, the risk function and internal audit.

    Type of stepProposed byApproved byChecked and recorded
    Accept the measurement as a basis for decisionsOperational RiskBusiness Control CommitteeModel Risk reviews the method. Operational Risk records the quarterly checks against reference risks and loss records.
    Fund the book of work by measured returnBCOBusiness Control CommitteeFinance challenges each project's cost and effect. Any exception to the ranking goes on file with its reason.
    Retire or simplify a control with a small effectControl ownerBCOOperational Risk challenges the proposal. The control owner records the evidence, monitoring indicator and reversal trigger.
    Retire or simplify a key control, change a control on one of the ten largest risks, or make any change that moves expected loss by $250k or moreControl ownerBusiness Control CommitteeThe same checks apply, with notification to Internal Audit.
    Accept a risk within appetiteRisk ownerBCOOperational Risk agrees to the acceptance, records it in the register and schedules a review after 12 months.
    Stop a programmeProgramme sponsorBCO and change governanceInternal Audit agrees how to close any related audit findings.
    Change a control that regulation requiresAny proposed change must strengthen the required control.

    BCO stands for Business Control Officer, the executive responsible for controls in the business. The reconstructed case has 44 main controls, including fifteen key controls used for financial reporting.

    Decision rules for the case

    • Control, testing and acceptance steps require an evidence threshold of at least 80% confidence that the step pays off, rising to 90% for retiring or simplifying a control. Projects follow measured return until the budget runs out. Each record states the estimated chance that the project pays off, and the committee records the reason for funding any project out of order.
    • The project ranking guides funding decisions. The committee can prioritize resilience or a regulatory commitment and records its reason for doing so.
    • Separate evidence supports each control’s effect, using tests, exception logs or a measurement with the control switched off.
    • Expected loss and bad-year loss stay within the risk appetite after every step.
    • Every control change or risk acceptance has a review trigger that uses a monitored indicator to reopen the decision when needed.
    • Cardinal re-measures the register every quarter. The bank checks each step against the new figures and compares them with the matrix ratings.

    The decision record identifies the evidence, approvers and reversal trigger. It gives the bank a documented explanation for a supervisor reviewing the change.

    A pilot on one of your registers

    A twelve-week pilot applies the method to one of your Payments risk registers, with Cardinal’s estimates alongside your current RCSA ratings. It uses your data to compare the existing assessment with the measurement and takes the first proposals to your committees.

    01 · Reproduce

    Measure the register

    Weeks 1 to 4

    We load your register, control list, book of work and loss events and measure the likelihood and cost of every risk. We then check the results against the losses you already know about.

    02 · Challenge

    Test the numbers

    Weeks 5 and 6

    Your process owners and Operational Risk challenge any comparison or reference risk that looks wrong. We gather evidence for control effects from your test results and exception logs.

    03 · Benchmark

    Compare the two views

    Weeks 7 and 8

    We set the measurement against your RCSA ratings, scenario analysis and loss history, risk by risk, and rank your book of work both ways.

    04 · Decide

    Take the first steps

    Weeks 9 to 12

    Your existing committees review the first candidate decisions. Agreed indicators and quarterly measurements track the approved changes.

    The pilot has review points at weeks 4 and 8. At week 4 you can assess the fit to reference risks and loss records, and the accuracy of comparisons with known answers. At week 8 you can compare project rankings and their estimated effect on the remediation budget. You decide at each point whether to continue.

    What we need from you

    • Your current Payments register with its RCSA ratings, the control list, the book of work and the loss events, in whatever form they exist today.
    • Test results and exception logs for the controls in scope.
    • Finance, as the source of the loss events and the project costs.
    • Two challenge sessions for each process area and one decision session with the BCO.

    What you get

    • A dollar estimate alongside each risk’s RCSA rating, including likelihood, loss per event, expected loss and an uncertainty range. The register-level calculation includes bad-year loss, as on the After page.
    • Your projects ranked by measured return, with an estimate of the remediation budget needed to match the existing plan’s protection, as on the Budget page.
    • A control ledger comparing the cost of each control with the loss it is expected to prevent, as on the Controls page.
    • Decision records for the first candidate steps, ready for your committees, as on the Steps page.
    • An account of the proposed financial effects by quarter, with spending changes and expected loss reductions shown separately, as on the Money page.

    How to assess the pilot

    The pilot tests the estimates against your own evidence. You can check recorded losses against each risk’s uncertainty interval, compare the projects selected by the two rankings, and assess control costs and effects using your test results and logs. The 65% benchmark in this case uses known values within the numerical reconstruction; establishing a saving at your bank requires its own evidence. If the rankings select similar projects, week 8 will show that agreement. Where they differ, you can examine the affected projects and the estimated loss reduction at the same budget. To begin, select a register and a sponsoring Business Control Officer, then ask Operational Risk and Finance for the data listed above.

The figures and sequences reflect that reconstruction. This page explains the numerical model and the research used to analyse it.
